Rule. An integral of a sum or difference of constant multiples splits into separate integrals, and constants move outside.
\(\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}\left[p\,f(x)+q\,g(x)\right]dx=p\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx+q\int_{a}^{b}g(x)\,dx\)
Original integral. We want
\(\displaystyle \int_{-6}^{-1}\left[3f(x)+h(x)\right]\,dx\)
Apply the rule. Split the integral and pull out the constants \(3\) and \(1\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{-6}^{-1}\left[3f(x)+h(x)\right]\,dx=3\int_{-6}^{-1}f(x)\,dx+\int_{-6}^{-1}h(x)\,dx\)
Substitute the numbers. \(\int_{-6}^{-1}f(x)\,dx=-5\) and \(\int_{-6}^{-1}h(x)\,dx=11\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{-6}^{-1}\left[3f(x)+h(x)\right]\,dx=3(-5)+(11)\)
Algebra. Multiply first, then add.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-6}^{-1}\left[3f(x)+h(x)\right]\,dx=-15+11=-4\)
Why it works. An integral is a limit of sums, and sums distribute over addition and constant multiples, so the integral does too.
Answer. \(-4\)

Algebra. The minus sign makes the value negative.

Rules. Use linearity to split the integral and pull out constants, reverse the limits to run left to right.
\(\displaystyle \int_{a}^{b}\left[p\,f+q\,g\right]dx=p\int_{a}^{b}f\,dx+q\int_{a}^{b}g\,dx\)
Original integral. We want
\(\displaystyle \int_{3}^{2}\left[-5f(x)+3h(x)\right]\,dx\)
Orient the given values. The rules below add integrals that run from left to right, so rewrite any given integral that runs backwards. Swapping the limits changes the sign: \(\int_{b}^{a}h(x)\,dx=-\int_{a}^{b}h(x)\,dx\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{2}^{3}f(x)\,dx=-\int_{3}^{2}f(x)\,dx=-12=-12\)
Apply linearity.
\(\displaystyle \int_{3}^{2}\left[-5f(x)+3h(x)\right]\,dx=-5\int_{3}^{2}f(x)\,dx+3\int_{3}^{2}h(x)\,dx\)
Reverse the limits. Each integral runs from \(3\) down to \(2\), so swap its limits and change its sign.
\(\displaystyle \int_{3}^{2}\left[-5f(x)+3h(x)\right]\,dx=-5\left(-\int_{2}^{3}f(x)\,dx\right)+3\left(-\int_{2}^{3}h(x)\,dx\right)\)
Substitute the numbers. \(\int_{2}^{3}f(x)\,dx=-12\) and \(\int_{2}^{3}h(x)\,dx=11\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{3}^{2}\left[-5f(x)+3h(x)\right]\,dx=-5(12)+3(-11)\)
Algebra. Multiply first, then add.
\(\displaystyle \int_{3}^{2}\left[-5f(x)+3h(x)\right]\,dx=-60-33=-93\)
Why it works. Integrals are limits of sums, so they split over addition, constants move outside, reversing the limits flips the sign of every term, and an interval is the sum of its pieces.
Answer. \(-93\)
